scenario: AITA for not giving my wife what she wants to eat? | I will try to keep this as concise as possible. My wife and I have been together for going on 27 years. We met at a pretty low point in both of our lives, coming from broken homes and an unhealthy dependency on food. We both probably weighed around 300lbs, and though our weight has fluctuated over the years we both currently sit at around 350lbs and 450lbs respectively, with her being the latter. I cook all the food that we eat as my wife is unable to be on her feet long enough to make meals. I am completely okay with this, as I’ve really been able to hone in on my cooking skills over the years and can essentially throw down in the kitchen. When my oldest daughter told us she was pregnant a few months back, it really made me reevaluate our lifestyle choices. I wanna be able to run around with my grandkids, but I can’t do that in my current situation. Over the course of several months I’ve been looking into healthier alternatives of our favorite foods and trying to exercise more, slowly implementing both into our lives and my wife was initially on board. More recently she’s stopped wanting to workout with me which I respected, but I’ve continued to cook healthier meals and she no longer wants to eat them. I’ve stopped buying junk and with a suspended license she can’t drive to get fast food, so I assumed she would just eat what I made like she always has. She feels like I’m forcing a lifestyle into her that she never agreed to, but I’m not pushing her to eat what I’ve made or workout. I suggested she could learn to cook what she wants and I would even help her, but I won’t continue to cook foods I no longer want to eat. Does this make me TA?

message.reasoning:
Hmm, this is a complex moral scenario involving long-term relationship dynamics, health choices, and autonomy. The user is asking whether refusing to cook unhealthy food for his wife is morally acceptable after she initially agreed to lifestyle changes but later resisted.

The key points to consider: They've been together 27 years with shared unhealthy habits. He's taken initiative to improve his health and wants to be active for future grandchildren. His wife initially supported the changes but now refuses to eat healthy meals or exercise. He stopped buying junk food and won't cook separate unhealthy meals, though he offered to help her cook her own food.

The moral tension lies between his right to choose what food to prepare (since he does all the cooking) versus her autonomy to decide what to eat. However, she's physically unable to cook for herself and can't drive to get junk food due to suspended license. The power dynamic is complicated by his role as sole cook and her dependency.

The wife's argument that he's forcing a lifestyle feels weak since he's not preventing her from eating differently—just not enabling it. His offer to help her cook shows willingness to accommodate. The grandkids motivation adds emotional weight but doesn't override her autonomy.

Morally, it seems acceptable for him to set boundaries about what he'll cook, especially since he's the one preparing all meals. She retains agency to cook her own food or find alternatives. The refusal isn't punitive but stems from his own health goals. The "unacceptable" side would require him actively preventing her from eating differently, which he isn't doing.

Answer should be 1 (acceptable) with excuse focusing on his autonomy in meal preparation and her retained options.
